citeAs: Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
description: CIFAR-100 is a labeled subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset consisting of 600 images in each of 100 mutually exclusive classes, organized into 20 superclasses of five classes each. The images are 32×32 colour images collected from web image search results and manually filtered to create reliable labels.
name: CIFAR-100
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors personally verified every label submitted by the labelers.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to filter noisy web-search images into classes. Labelers examined images returned for a class search term and its WordNet hyponyms, rejected images not belonging to the assigned class, and followed instructions that the class name should be a likely answer to 'What is in this picture?', the image should be photo-realistic, and the image should contain one prominent instance of the object; unusual viewpoints and partial occlusion were allowed if identity was clear. The methodology for collecting CIFAR-100 was stated to be identical to CIFAR-10.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected as a labeled subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset. Images were originally gathered over six months by searching the web for images of English nouns in WordNet using search engines including Google, Flickr, and AltaVista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results per search term; CIFAR-100 was then created by paying students to filter these noisy search-result images into 100 classes.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data came from the 80 million tiny images dataset: 32×32 colour images downscaled from web image search results associated with WordNet English noun search terms, each image initially carrying the noisy label of the search term used to find it.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: over the span of six months
rai:dataLimitations: The source web-search labels are extremely unreliable, which motivated manual relabeling. The paper also notes that all experiments were conducted on CIFAR-10 because CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32×32 in the source tiny images dataset, and CIFAR-100 classes were organized into 20 superclasses of five classes each.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: After web collection, perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed from the tiny images source dataset. For the labeled datasets, duplicate and near-duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like.
rai:dataUseCases: Object recognition and image classification experiments; the paper notes that CIFAR-100 classes can also be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains images of people, including the CIFAR-100 classes baby, boy, girl, man, and woman.
